sourceNote: Synthetic stress-test case in the B2B SaaS domain, built with realistic, internally-consistent SaaS metrics (ARR, growth, churn, NRR, CAC/LTV, adoption, sales-cycle, and support signals). The intended root-cause diagnosis is withheld from this visible input; the owner intake intentionally frames the problem in the owner's own words, and the engine must trace the evidence to the true root cause without being told the answer. Not a historical case; all figures are representative.

ownerIntake.businessType: Vertical SaaS for production planning and scheduling sold to discrete-manufacturing firms. Annual contracts, $30k-$120k ACV, implementation-heavy onboarding. Founded 2020, Series B raised 2024. ARR $8M, 130 customers, ~70 employees.
ownerIntake.stage: ARR $8M, 40% YoY growth but decelerating; churn 3% MRR; CAC $35k; LTV $180k; LTV:CAC ~5.1:1; gross margin 80%. Cash runway 36 months. ~90% of customers and new-logo ARR concentrated in the core discrete-manufacturing vertical.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Series B expansion with focus on deeper penetration of the core manufacturing vertical and a path to $20M ARR within 18 months, while protecting capital efficiency.
ownerConstraints: Sales constraint: Limited sales resources (8 quota-carrying reps); cannot dramatically expand headcount without straining the 36-month runway and capital-efficiency expectations.
Product constraint: Each new vertical or sub-segment requires meaningful vertical-specific customization and integrations (8-12 weeks of product/engineering effort per adjacency).
Market constraint: The core discrete-manufacturing segment the company targets is finite; signals suggest the reachable, qualified portion of that segment is approaching saturation.
Data constraint: The company tracks ARR, churn, and CAC/LTV by vertical and customer count by industry, but has no validated market-size or addressable-demand estimate by vertical or sub-segment.
Organizational constraint: Lean go-to-market and customer-success teams; entering an adjacent vertical would require new domain expertise and reference customers the company does not yet have.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Growth is slowing: YoY growth is 40% but month-over-month new-bookings growth has fallen from ~5% to ~3.5%, and win rates in the core segment are softening as the most obvious target accounts have already been sold. The concern is whether the company has nearly exhausted the qualified demand in its core vertical (a saturation/forecast problem), is losing deals to competitors, or has hit a product-market-fit ceiling. Leadership is leaning toward investing further in the same vertical, but lacks any addressable-demand estimate to confirm headroom remains.

businessProblem: A Series B vertical-SaaS company is experiencing growth deceleration with an unclear root cause: core-segment saturation versus competitive displacement versus a product-market-fit ceiling. YoY growth is 40% but MoM new-bookings growth has slowed (~5% to ~3.5%) and core-segment win rates are softening as the most obvious accounts are already sold. Roughly 90% of customers sit in a single discrete-manufacturing vertical the company has no addressable-demand estimate for. Leadership wants to invest further in the same vertical, but cannot say how much qualified demand remains. The central question is whether the company has been planning growth against an over-optimistic forecast of reachable demand in its core segment, and whether the right move is deeper core penetration, an adjacent-vertical expansion, or a competitive-positioning fix.

evidence.finding: YoY growth is 40% but MoM new-bookings growth has decelerated from ~5% (run-rate ~80% annualized) to ~3.5% (~51% annualized), and the trend is still slowing. The deceleration is in new bookings, not in retention, pointing to a top-of-funnel demand or acquisition issue rather than a churn problem.

Approximately 90% of customers and new-logo ARR are concentrated in the core discrete-manufacturing vertical. Win rates in that segment have softened over the trailing year (from ~28% to ~22%) and sales cycles have lengthened, consistent with the most obvious, best-fit accounts already being sold and the remaining pipeline being lower-quality.
evidence.source: Pipeline and win-rate analysis by segment

evidence.finding: Churn is steady at 3% MRR and net revenue retention is healthy (~112%) with strong expansion inside existing accounts. Retention and product satisfaction are not deteriorating, which localizes the growth problem to acquisition/demand rather than to product value or a retention failure.

Unit economics remain strong: CAC $35k, LTV $180k, LTV:CAC ~5.1:1, gross margin 80%. The economics are not broken; the issue is that the volume of new qualified opportunities in the core vertical is shrinking, not that each deal has become unprofitable. No validated addressable-demand model exists to confirm how much qualified core-segment demand remains.
evidence.source: CAC/LTV analysis; absence of addressable-demand model
